email.scenario: You spent last Saturday at the Elm Street Historical Society learning how to catalog donated letters as a new volunteer. While shelving items afterward, you noticed a diary from the 1920s that had recently been donated was sitting without any acid-free protective sleeve.
email.subject: Saturday's Orientation and a Diary I Noticed
bullets: Thank the collections manager for Saturday's cataloging orientation.
Describe the 1920s donated diary you found without a protective sleeve.
Ask that a protective sleeve be added before the diary is handled further.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: Many fitness centers are considering requiring members to reserve specific time slots for popular exercise machines during peak hours, rather than allowing first-come, first-served access. Supporters say this would guarantee everyone a fair chance to use the equipment they need. Critics worry it would eliminate the flexibility to drop in whenever a schedule allows. Should fitness centers require reservation slots for exercise machines during peak hours? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Maya
studentPosts.post: I think reservation slots make sense during peak hours. Right now I sometimes wait twenty minutes just to use a squat rack, and a reservation system would guarantee me access instead of hoping the machine opens up. As long as slots aren't too long, most members could still fit a workout into their schedule.

studentPosts.name: Dmitri
studentPosts.post: I understand Maya's frustration with the wait, but reservations would ruin what I like most about the gym: dropping in whenever I have a free hour between classes. If I had to book ahead, I'd probably skip workouts on busy weeks instead of just going when I could.
